summary: Edward Said, Ranajit Guha and Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak become person entries. Said: Orientalism and contrapuntal reading (1978–93) to postcolonial history, Foucault's and Gramsci's influence, critiques of Foucault (empire left out), of Marx on India (contested) and of world history as historicism (1985), the 1988 foreword to Subaltern Studies and the resistance culture of Culture and Imperialism (1993). Guha: the Subaltern Studies programme (1982–83), insurgency as politics (1983), critiques of elitist nationalist historiography, of Hobsbawm's 'pre-political' (1983) and of Thompson's 'rule of law' (1989), Gramsci's influence, and his influence on Chakrabarty. Spivak: 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' (1985–99), a critique of Subaltern Studies from within (strategic essentialism and the gendered subaltern), a critique of Foucault (1988), Derrida's influence and her influence on Chakrabarty. Six group edges that named one of them are relabelled to the distinct collective or later intervention each records: edge_604 (Chatterjee, 1986), edge_357, edge_114 (now a contribution), edge_389 (Nair 1990; the series in 1996), edge_025 (Prakash, 1992) and edge_386 (Stoler, 1995). Some overlap between group and person edges remains and is acknowledged: edge_024 and edge_385 (Said's uses of Foucault and Gramsci), edge_107 (Said's and Spivak's textual routes) and edge_159 (Gramsci through Guha).
authorization: User, 2026-10-14: Chakrabarty 'should connect to subalteran studies and E. P. Thompson ... maybe a few other key people?'; 'yes Said is essential'. Said, Guha and Spivak now; Bhabha and Chatterjee later.
rationale: Person entries go to thinkers whose frameworks students meet across fields (user, 2026-10-13). Said's Orientalism, Guha's subaltern programme and Spivak's question of subaltern speech are read across postcolonial history, Subaltern Studies, gender, labour and world history. Chakrabarty became a person entry in 1.132 with no incoming edges; Guha and Spivak supply them on read evidence. Each draft's NOTES.md records what was read in full, in part, through reviewers or reprints, and what was not read (among them Ahmad's In Theory, Parry 1987, Clifford 1980, Rule of Property and the 1997 Dominance without Hegemony). In-period critics are kept: al-'Azm and Lewis on Said, with Clifford (1980) recorded but unread and Ahmad known only as reported; O'Hanlon, Bayly, Sarkar and Spivak herself on Guha; O'Hanlon and Eagleton criticise Spivak, while Prakash and Sarkar credit her sati discussion, and Parry (1987) is recorded but unread. Dissertation evidence is metadata only and never in entry text.

edge_604.relationship: Chatterjee extends the Subaltern critique from nationalist historiography to nationalist thought as a 'derivative discourse' (1986)
edge_604.evidence_note: Guha's 1982 statement (read) opened the critique of elite historiography; his own critique is the separate edge from his person entry. This edge records the distinct extension to nationalist thought. Sarkar (1997, pp. 91–92, read), a former member, traces how Partha Chatterjee's Nationalist Thought and the Colonial World (1986) carried the critique to the colonized intelligentsia's 'derivative discourses', and objects that 'A project that had started with a trenchant attack on elite nationalist historiography had now chosen as its hero the principal iconic figure of official Indian nationalism' (p. 92). Later reading, labelled: Chakrabarty (2000, p. 25) writes that Chatterjee's book 'extended Guha's criticisms of nationalist historiography into a full-blown, brilliant critique of nationalist thought itself'. The arrow does not claim a denial of all national histories.

edge_357.relationship: Subaltern Studies essays treat peasant, tribal and worker action under colonial rule as politics with its own forms, and are criticised for overstating its autonomy (1982–88)
edge_357.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, pp. 86–87, read against the page images) lists early work that explored 'popular or subaltern autonomy in action, consciousness and culture': Hardiman on the peasant nationalists of Gujarat, Pandey on Congress organization and peasant militancy, Amin on rumours of Gandhi, studies of 'tribal movements and cults' and of Bengal labour. Bayly (1988; Verso reprint pp. 116–126, read) finds the essays' empirical work strong but holds that 'their concern to emphasize peasant autonomy seems to have deflected them from moving towards a “total history”' (p. 121) and that 'Simply to stress that autonomy ... is not very helpful in any attempt to specify the nature of historical change' (p. 126). O'Hanlon (1988; reprint pp. 85–86) criticises the 'literal interpretation of subaltern autonomy' in several contributions (Henningham, Ramachandra Guha, Dasgupta) while setting Ranajit Guha's book apart (p. 85). Ranajit Guha's own argument is the separate edge from his person entry.

edge_114.relationship: Subaltern Studies modifies the historiography of anti-colonial nationalism through an emphasis on 'pressures from below' and popular initiative beyond elite leadership (1982–88)
edge_114.evidence_note: Sarkar (1997, p. 86, read against the page image): the group's publications 'helped to significantly modify the historiography of anticolonial nationalism through a common initial emphasis on “pressures from below”', citing Hardiman, Pandey and Amin; it had been argued 'with considerable justice by Guha and other contributors' that anti-colonial movements had been explained 'far too often' by economic pressures and mobilization from the top (p. 85). He also notes that the critique of nationalist leaders restraining mass initiative 'had been quite common in some kinds of Marxist writing, most notably in R. P. Dutt's India Today' (p. 86, n. 8). The challenge concerns elite nationalist historiography, not every liberation movement or anti-colonial history.

edge_389.relationship: Feminist critics press Subaltern Studies on women's place in its accounts of labour and community (Nair, 1990), and gender becomes a theme of the series (1996)
edge_389.evidence_note: Janaki Nair's 1990 review in International Labor and Working-Class History questions Chakrabarty's treatment of gender in Bengal labour (graph verification note; gender strand bengal_labor_gender; not re-read here). Spivak's own 1985–88 critique is the separate edge from her person entry (revision 1.137); this edge records Nair's 1990 criticism and the series' 1996 uptake. Vinayak Chaturvedi (2000, p. xviii, n. 46, read) writes that 'Can the Subaltern Speak?' 'brought issues of gender to the forefront of Subaltern Studies' and that Subaltern Studies IX (1996) made 'gender issues' a dominant theme, with Kamala Visweswaran's 'Small Speeches, Subaltern Gender' and Susie Tharu and Tejaswini Niranjana's 'Problems for a Contemporary Theory of Gender' (both unread). Spivak (2000, p. 325, read) names Tharu as the member whose work is informed by feminist theory. The arrow records criticism and its uptake within the series; it does not claim that the collective adopted a feminist programme.

edge_025.relationship: Prakash defends deconstruction for postcolonial historical writing against O'Hanlon and Washbrook's charge of a 'residual positivism' (1992)
edge_025.evidence_note: Gyan Prakash, 'Can the “Subaltern” Ride?' (CSSH 1992; Verso reprint, pp. 224–227, read), defends deconstruction for historical writing under the heading 'Deconstructive Criticism and Historical Writing', reading Derrida's Of Grammatology and 'White Mythology' and answering O'Hanlon and Washbrook, who, as he quotes them, charge it with a 'residual positivism' and, in his paraphrase, with treating the historian's intervention in the past as illegitimate (p. 225, citing their p. 198, 2000 reprint pagination). O'Hanlon and Washbrook's own text is known here only through its first page and notes (pe132_ohanlon_washbrook_1992) and through Prakash's quotations. Rosalind O'Hanlon (1988; reprint p. 80, read) reads the Subaltern series' recovery of the subject as a 'strategy' whose 'limitations have yet to receive any proper public discussion'. Spivak's own use is the separate derrida → Spivak edge.

edge_386.relationship: Stoler questions the marginal place of race and empire in Foucault's history of sexuality while using his 1976 lectures (1995)
edge_386.map_label: Stoler: race, sexuality and empire in Foucault, 1995
edge_386.evidence_note: The checked publisher description of Race and the Education of Desire (1995) records a critique of the marginal place of empire, and of race in the making of bourgeois sexuality, in Foucault alongside productive use of his 1976 lectures and Dutch and French colonial archives; the book itself is unread. Spivak's critique of Foucault is the separate edge from her person entry.
